newsitem.title: USA: Court rejects challenge to Oregon right-to-die law.
newsitem.headline: Court rejects challenge to Oregon right-to-die law.

text.p: A federal appeals court threw out Thursday a lawsuit challenging Oregon's so-called "Death with Dignity Act," which allows doctor-assisted suicide for the terminally ill.
The 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals said the lawsuit brought by a group of patients, doctors and nursing homes should be dismissed because they lacked standing.
The appeals court ruled doctors and terminally ill patients must allege "concrete and imminent injury" in order to challenge the constitutionality of a state's "right-to-die" statute.
The attorneys that challenged Oregon's Measure 16, the Death with Dignity Act, said the appeals court decision was flawed and vowed to file an appeal.
"There are very strong constitutional arguments against Measure 16," plaintiffs attorney Richard Coleson said. "Those arguments were not considered by the 9th Circuit."
The Hemlock Society USA, a Denver-based organisation that supports doctor-assisted suicide, hailed the appeals court decision.
"I hope that we'll see the Oregon law go into effect as quickly as possible so it will be a model for the rest of the country," Hemlock Society Executive Director Faye Girsh said.
Opponents of assisted suicide blasted the ruling.

"The ... decision demonstrates the urgency of the state of Oregon acting promptly to repeal this misguided and deadly law," Burke Balch, a director at the National Right to Life Committee, said in a statement.
The Oregon Death with Dignity Act was approved by the state's voters in 1994.
It allows terminally ill adults who are mentally competent to ask for a prescription for medication "for the purpose of ending his or her life in a humane and dignified manner."

But 15 days before the measure was to take effect, a group of doctors, patients and nursing homes challenged it in federal court, alleging the act violated the U.S. Constitution and several federal statutes.

The judge in Oregon hearing the case issued an injunction against the measure. The district court found that the Death with Dignity Act did not provide enough safeguards to prevent an incompetent terminally ill adult from committing suicide.
But the appeals court set aside that ruling.

The appeals court said federal courts had no jurisdiction to hear the case, finding the plaintiffs had no legal standing to file their lawsuit because they did not show they were in danger of "imminent" harm from the law.
The three-judge panel ordered the district court to dismiss the lawsuit. It did not, however, address the constitutionality of the Oregon law in its ruling.

"It's gratifying to see the state's position affirmed in the court, but there are still some issues to be resolved," said Peter Cogswell, a spokesman for Oregon's attorney general. "We're not at the end of this lawsuit."
